model:claude|title:how the claude code t.content_excerpt: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude . At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens. You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again. So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team. If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes. If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page. model:glm|title:glm models cut ai coding.content_excerpt: Revolut serves 80 million customers across 45 markets, and a secondary share sale that closed in July 2026 valued it at $115 billion, making it Europe's most valuable private company. It also, according to the man who runs its AI operations, now spends about one-tenth on AI coding tokens what it used to pay Anthropic and OpenAI. The blended cost of running self-hosted GLM models is 30 cents per million tokens, David Abitbol said on the AI Engineer podcast — and that single number is quietly rewriting how a regulated bank buys artificial intelligence. The striking part is not the discount. It is that Revolut reached it by doing less: fewer GPUs than the workload would seem to demand, less context than the models advertise, less precision than the hardware allows, and fewer permissions than an autonomous agent would want. Constraint, not capacity, turned out to be the lever. Revolut's numbers come from a sample of 2,000 engineers tracked over roughly a year, which makes them unusual — most enterprises deploying AI assistants have no clean before-and-after. The first rollout, Gemini in January 2025, delivered a 10% improvement in lead time and 20% in coding time. Abitbol credits the coding gain to engineers no longer digging through Stack Overflow and documentation. Claude Code was trialed around February 2025 and launched at scale in January 2026, but showed little measurable impact at first — and the cost raised eyebrows. Engineers were spending $1,000 to $10,000 a month with weak returns, so the rollout arrived with strict budget caps. Self-hosting open-source models from around April 2026 changed the picture. GLM 5.1 at that point delivered a 60% improvement in coding time and 70% in lead time. The asymmetry is the insight. The larger gain landed on lead time, not coding time, because writing code was never the bottleneck. "What we find is the bottleneck for engineering is not necessarily coding," Abitbol said. "You can save a lot of time not having to dig through your inbox or messing with Jira and Confluence." There is a second-order effect that does not show up in the table. When tokens are effectively unlimited, engineers stop rationing them — saving the expensive tool for the end of the quarter or the hardest task — and start using it on everything. Abitbol's posture now is blunt: open source is the priority, billing is flat with no month-to-month bill shock, and frontier models are the exception. story|title:a benchmark that diffs the w.content_excerpt: Benchmark for computer-use agents on self-hosted business apps, graded by whole-database diffs: success, collateral damage, irreversible changes, false completion. A benchmark that checks what a computer-use agent actually did to the database, not what it said it did. Agents drive real, self-hosted business apps (Invoice Ninja, Dolibarr, Odoo 17, Odoo 18) in a browser. Every episode starts from the same database snapshot, and afterwards the whole database is diffed . That gives four verdicts per episode instead of one: Agents: GPT-6 Luna (accessibility tree + screenshot) and UI-TARS-1.5-7B (screenshot only), same harness, 30-step budget. Full write-up with every table, the failure taxonomy and the limitations: reports/phase0_writeup.md . These are small-sample results from one person's Phase 0: 36 to 72 episodes per cell, one run per task, Wilson 95% intervals. Read Limitations before quoting a number. You need Docker, Python 3.10 to 3.12 (or uv , which fetches one for you), and about 8 GB of free disk. Check the published numbers without running anything (rebuilds every table from the committed episode summaries: 635 scored, plus 35 superseded ones kept for a sensitivity check): swm up takes about six minutes the first time (image download and seeding). In Phase 0, GPT-6 Luna cost one to three cents per successful task. Each episode writes screenshots, the step log and a summary.json under runs/<tag>/<task>/ . Apps: invoiceninja · dolibarr · odoo17 · odoo18 . Everything binds to 127.0.0.1 , agents cannot navigate off localhost, and no real email can be sent. A custom agent is one class with one method. It returns a BrowserGym action string: The diff lives in swm/dbdiff.py (about 90 lines, MySQL and Postgres). What counts as a legitimate change for each task is in swm/tasks_*.py . Clean condition. Full table with perturbations and per-skill breakdown: reports/phase0_results.md . Neither agent was trained on any of these apps, so this table measures app difficulty, not transfer. State-based grading of agents is an active area. Agent-Diff diffs full environment state for API agents on Slack, Linear, Box and Calendar replicas. EntWorld verifies enterprise GUI agents by querying Odoo and EspoCRM databases. WebArena and WorkArena are the standard web-agent benchmarks, and this harness is built on BrowserGym . What this repo adds is the same tasks across two major versions of one app , with collateral and irreversible changes reported separately from success. Ne

story|title:a browser api for choosing a.content_excerpt: navigator.models is a proposed browser API for web apps that need a particular open-weight model on-device. A workflow built around one model may not work with another. Apps should be able to ask for the model they built and tested against, regardless of which browser someone uses. Web Models makes that request explicit. The page names a model ID. The browser runs that model or tells the page it can’t. There is no quiet fallback. The best model for scanning a receipt, transcribing audio, and searching documents may differ. A model ID lets a developer ask for the same model and release in any browser. Some models take gigabytes to download and plenty of memory to run. The browser can share their weights across sites, so every site does not need to download and store another copy. An app asks for a model, and the browser asks the user. They can see and revoke access for each site and model. The browser also keeps an eye on setup, execution, and resource limits. When someone searches their notes or documents, they should not have to send them to a model provider. Local inference can keep that data on-device and work offline when the model and content are already there. Your app picks the model and calls the API. The user grants access. The browser runs it. This is just illustrative JavaScript. <model-id> is a placeholder. Your app provides button , output , and showFallback() . The first access request has to start with a user gesture. This page does not run a model. For a one-off task, make a direct call. If you will use the model again, keep it in a session. Your app still owns the conversation history. Once access is granted, the browser tells you what that model supports. Vision, audio, tools, structured output, reasoning, and embeddings all depend on the model you chose. Each ID is tied to fixed weights, a tokenizer, and default input and generation settings. A changed release gets a new ID, so developers decide when to move to it. Shared catalogs, model retirement, and cross-browser compatibility tests are still open questions. Open an example to see the code. The model IDs are placeholders; replace them with the specific model IDs your app uses. Here, documentInput is a text area containing the article or document. button , output , and showFallback() are supplied by your app. These examples are illustrative and do not execute on this page. story|title:ai agents attempted exploits.content_excerpt: Three events in October 2026 involving Trajectory Labs, PBC, and our recommendations for evaluators In late October, three events occurred during alignment evals run by Trajectory Labs, PBC (Trajectory) in which AI agents — identified by Trajectory as publicly available frontier models — interacted with Epoch employees and the Epoch website. Trajectory is an organization that builds safety evals and conducts red-teaming of frontier models. To avoid misattributing behavior, this report does not name any AI models or developers, as Epoch AI has not independently verified which were involved. The first event, which occurred without Epoch’s approval or prior notice from Trajectory, involved agents attempting multiple exploits, including an SQL injection, and contacting Epoch employees under false identities to try to obtain proprietary Epoch benchmark information. This behavior appears to have resulted, at least in part, from Trajectory giving the agents an intentionally impossible task and instructions not to give up or conclude the task was impossible. The second event involved renewed agent activity on our public website, which Trajectory attributed to agents getting past a DNS redirect that Trajectory had set up to keep them on a local copy of Epoch’s site. In the third event, Epoch collaborated with Trajectory on an alignment experiment similar to the first event. Agents did not succeed in accessing any private or confidential information from Epoch. On the evening of October 20, 2026, Epoch employees noticed a spike in agent activity on Epoch’s website. Specifically, we detected a high volume of activity on a planted API endpoint designed to monitor for malicious engagement with our website. We launched the planted API endpoint on October 5, 2026, and it received periodic traffic from agents seeking benchmark scores. The planted API endpoint did not connect to any private data on our website. During the increased activity on October 20, we deployed an “agent hotline” to let agents send short messages to Epoch staff. Between 4:30pm and 7:30pm Pacific Time, agents sent 487 messages and made 36,411 calls to the planted API. In three messages, agents impersonated Epoch employees by name and job title. In 27 messages, agents claimed to be engineers or auditors. In three messages, agents claimed to be an AI assistant from a frontier lab. In 17 messages, agents claimed to be an “internal AI model,” an assertion apparently derived from Trajectory’s system prompt

story|title:benchmarking oss inference v.content_excerpt: This repo is in beta. We're still iterating on the methodology, so the approach and results may change. These results show speed (time to complete a research task) and cost for a single agent, not performance under heavy load, and providers differ in ways these tests won't capture. How fast and how cheap is each inference provider at serving an AI research agent using open-source LLMs? We record each model doing a set of research tasks once, using questions from Google's FRAMES benchmark, then replay those conversations on every provider. We measure how long the model calls take and what they cost at list price . Every model provider gets the same set of requests for a given model and task, so we're testing how each provider serves the model, not the model's ability to complete the task well. This is not a benchmark of model quality. Every model here completes every task, and we don't check whether its answers are right. The purpose of this benchmark is to compare timing and cost across providers, not model intelligence. Each model answers a set of multi-hop questions from FRAMES as a research agent, with tools to search and read Wikipedia. We only use tasks that every model is able to finish, and save each model's conversations along with the Wikipedia responses. The benchmark replays those conversations. For each turn, we send the conversation up to that point to the provider, time the response, and move on to the next recorded turn. The Wikipedia results come from the recording, so the timings only include model calls. Each model works through the tasks differently, so results are only comparable between providers serving the same model. Every provider gets the same settings for a given model (minimal reasoning, and temperature 0). After an untimed warm-up request, each provider handles one request at a time. Time spent waiting on rate limits isn't counted. Caching works normally within a task, and to see how much it helps, we also resend each task's last turn without the conversation cached. Each run goes through every task several times. A task that fails gets retried, and we only publish a run if every task finished. We run the benchmark monthly and on request, and the charts average every run from the last 30 days. Some runs only cover one provider, so providers may be measured on different days. Cost is the list price for the tokens each provider reports. Credits and discounts aren't included. Contributions are welcome. Feel free to open an issue o

story|title:build a real time next best.content_excerpt: Author a Feature once, serve it everywhere — one declarative definition powers point-in-time training and warm online ranking at p95 34 ms, with in-session signals live in under 130 ms. Real-time personalization depends on understanding what customers want in the moment. When a retail banking customer checks their accounts, explores credit cards, or opens a loan calculator, each interaction signals their current intent. A relevant offer needs to reach them while they're still in the session. The challenge is making that intent available to the model. Raw clickstream data must be aggregated into time-windowed features for two purposes: training on historical values as they existed at a given point in time, and serving predictions using current values with millisecond latency. Building these pipelines separately creates duplicate feature definitions that can drift over time and degrade model accuracy. Databricks Feature Views solve this by letting you define features once for both training and serving. In this blog, we'll walk through an open-source Solution Accelerator that uses Feature Views to build a real-time next-best-offer (NBO) recommender for financial services. The accelerator includes two parts: a recommender using batch features and an extension that adds streaming, in-session intent. Both are built end-to-end on Databricks, with runnable notebooks you can clone and deploy. Real-time recommendations require both consistency and speed. Features must be computed the same way during training and serving to avoid train/serve skew, which can degrade model accuracy. At inference time, those features must also be retrieved and scored in milliseconds. Traditionally, meeting both requirements meant maintaining separate systems: a batch pipeline for training features and a hand-written streaming job for online serving. This creates duplicate logic that can drift over time. Feature Views eliminate the need for separate feature definitions. You declare the logic once, and Databricks reuses it across training and serving: At training time, the create_training_set API retrieves feature values as they existed at each labeled event, preventing future data leakage. At inference time, the Model Serving endpoint fetches batch features from the online store using customer_id . story|title:dawn of the super agent.content_excerpt: A few months ago if you'd asked me if an agent could run Agno, I would have said NO. Impossible. Too many moving parts. The system was too complex, I hated the writing style, and we had to be involved in the design decisions. But around september, we noticed a step change improvement in how coding agents made decisions. They went off on fewer tangents, made better design decisions and were more thorough in their work. Astra's even half-decent at writing docs. I started trusting them with more ambitious work. Now I use one super-session to coordinate everything. I still run my agents manually, pass context between them, check for reviews and take things to the finish line. But that one long-running super-session is my partner in crime. Now the question is: can I hand over this coordination to a super-agent? Can a super-agent eventually run Agno for me? I'm at the beginning of this journey so if your team is spending more and more time managing agents, follow along. A Super Agent sits on top of your coding agents and coordinates their work. You give it an outcome, it figures out what to do, which agents to use and how to get it done. Today I do all of this manually. It makes sense to take this step by step, so here's what I'd consider a success for Super Agent v1: This is a big time sink that super can take over. I do most of my development using coding agents. Claude or codex will write the spec, I'll review the design, they'll implement it and run tests. story|title:from tasks to goals.content_excerpt: As agents become more powerful, we’re moving from giving them tasks to giving them goals. Under the hood, this move from tasks to goals consists of two more practical shifts: This is changes what an agent does, what it needs, how its built, and we interact with it. Previously, the user would specify tasks. Now, the user specifies a goal, and the agent iterates towards that goal by deconstructing into tasks, doing some of them, updating the task list, etc. The agent needs to be good at brainstorming and selecting different tasks, which requires new context engineering and prompting strategies. It needs to be somewhat creative - and varied - in brainstorming potential tasks (if it keeps on suggesting the same tasks over and over again, that’s not great). Practical consideration: you need some way to see what tasks the agent is doing (e.g. a to-do list), as well as prompting for the agent to be creative in coming up with tasks When you give an agent task, you largely have an idea of what tools it will call. When you give it a goal - you don’t really know what tools it will call, and you may not even know what tools it will need to call. Practical consideration: you need more controls over what tools an agent can or cannot call When you give an agent a task, you’re naturally in the loop. If you don’t provide all the information up front, its easy for the agent to ask follow up questions in chat. When you give an agent a goal - it may be running in the background and need to get clarification on certain points. It needs a way to ask questions to humans - whether through Slack or a dedicated UI. Practical consideration: you need a mechanism for a background agent to ask you for clarification The agent needs to know how its doing as it progresses towards a goal. This could either be by checking in on a metric to see if it is improving, or by getting explicit feedback from a human on how its doing. The more closely tied to a metric, the better in some sense (easy for it to track automatically!) but its never wise to blindly optimize a metric, so explicit human feedback may be the best thing. This is why its important to design goals in a way where its easy to give feedback. You can have both metrics for the agent to drive towards, and a way to get feedback from users. story|title:gavel guided code review wit.content_excerpt: Review local Git changes in your browser with Claude Code or Codex . The gavel skill tells your agent to prepare a brief, explain its choices beside the code, and guide you through the diff. Large changes are split into focused reviews, so you have less context to hold in your head at once. Ask questions in threads, request revisions, and give each part a verdict. As a background task, I’ve been working for … longer than I’d like to admit on the task of adding authentication and authorization to PhotoStructure. The fourth (!!) dev spike was the charm—the first three attempts left me with a pretty solid set of specifications to guide the implementation. I wrote the db schema and the onboarding flow. Claude and Codex helped flesh out the implementation over several hundred sessions, coordinated with technical project plans . I reviewed every change before committing it. And it’s been a slog . It’s a given that authentication and authorization are going to be hard. But I felt like my reviewing approach kinda sucked had a lot of opportunity for improvement. It’s a bit of a PITA. My brain only has so many thinks it can think in a day. Any friction to giving the robot feedback, especially as your brain fades, can let “fuck it, ship it” creep in. I was explaining this to my wife during a walk, and realized that there was a better way. At a prior job at a Big Company, I helped interns get their PRs approved and merged by having them write a narrative around their diffs . This approach helps walk the reviewer through the PR, and is way better than the asciibetical sort order of staged diffs and a proposed git commit message that I’d been slogging through. The reviewer spends their limited cognitive mojo on judging the PR, not on basic orientation and background arcana. If the agent could write a “brief” for every review–just a sentence or three–and then add linked comments through the diffs to walk me through the changes, each review would be much simpler to digest and wrap my brain around. But, ugh, agents still work via a glorified chat interface. The Codex and Claude desktop apps, for example, each have a diff tool, but neither threads your comments. Juggling multiple issues simultaneously in one review is work . I’ve also seen the Codex diff viewer get confused and show irrelevant diffs from other worktrees. story|title:harness evals compare agent.content_excerpt: Evaluate an agent harness or workflow with the model held fixed: use-case tasks, repeated trials, hard checks, paired comparisons. A small Python library for evaluating an agent harness or a workflow with the model held fixed. You describe your use case as tasks with checks, connect each harness through a short adapter, and get repeated-run metrics with intervals: success, reliability, cost, latency and model usage. It plots the designs on two metrics at once, marks the ones no other design beats on both, and decides whether to adopt, reject or keep investigating a change. It is the companion code for the article on evaluating agent harnesses in the Recursive Harness Engineering series. The agent-harness-lab installs it to evaluate five designs of one support assistant, from a plain agent to a workflow with no agent. Two figures answer the questions a table cannot: which harness gives the best trade-off, and where each one fails. The example runs offline in a second. It is in the repository, not in the installed package: It prints the table and the decision shown below , and saves the runs and both figures to out/ . Its "agent" is a simulated model with seeded mistakes, so the numbers describe the simulation only. The same results from the saved runs: A model benchmark keeps the harness fixed and changes the model. A harness evaluation does the opposite: the model, its endpoint and settings, the tasks and the checks stay fixed, and only the harness changes. Then a difference in the results belongs to the harness. This is a template: Environment , run_my_agent and my_workflow stand for your code. examples/refund_desk.py is the runnable version. summarize takes the grades of one harness. Pass USECASE.metrics , or your own metrics are left out. did , never , at_most , says , never_says , ended , state and judged cover the common obligations. For anything else, wrap your own function in a Check : Return a real True or False : None means the evidence is missing and is reported as undecided, so write bool(re.search(...)) , not re.search(...) . A check that raises or returns any other type is undecided too. This also applies to saved state and judge verdicts: strings such as "false" cannot pass. never and at_most are critical by default and the others are not; pass critical=True or critical=False to change that. Since May 2026, a new flagship proprietary or open-weight model has launched roughly every week, or every 3.7 days when regional labs are included. The Index tracks model adoption through token and spend shares across proprietary and open-weight models, as well as weekly AI spending patterns for individual users. story|title:sasy agent policies in decla.content_excerpt: SASY checks each action an AI agent takes, such as sending an email or running a command, before it happens. You write the policy as rules in Datalog, a declarative logic language. Each decision takes into account everything that led to that action, from what the agent read to the tools it called. Both runs below give an agent the same task: summarize a report and email the summary to reviewer@example.net. In the second run, the agent also reads an untrusted note telling it to send the summary somewhere else. Your agent runs as before. The SASY SDK records what it reads and produces, and the SASY engine checks each tool call against your policy and that history before it runs. A denied call does not run, and the agent gets the reason. The SDK hooks into LangChain, Google ADK and Langroid automatically. Custom agents use sasy.record and sasy.check_tool_call . Docs Architecture → Blog Agentic Security: An Aspect-Oriented Programming Perspective → Let a coding agent set SASY up for you, or install it by hand in a Python project. The documentation explains how to write policies and add SASY to each framework. A real run of the message-flow example. An agent is asked to email a reviewer a summary of a confidential report. On the way, it reads an untrusted note telling it to send the summary elsewhere, and follows it. That email depends on both the note and the report, and the policy blocks it. The graph is what SASY records for the run. When the agent tries the send, SASY follows the arrows back to both documents, and the policy denies it. SASY Guard brings SASY to the coding agent on your machine. It checks every tool call against a policy and the session's history. story|title:tabular foundation models on.content_excerpt: Run and fine-tune tabular foundation models using fully managed, on-demand GPUs integrated with your Databricks data and ML workflows. by Marc Susagna Holgado , Javier Poveda Panter , Puneet Jain and Ryuta Yoshimatsu Many of the most valuable predictive machine learning applications rely on tabular data. From credit risk and customer churn to demand forecasting and predictive maintenance, these use cases have traditionally required teams to develop, train and maintain models for each prediction task. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) offer another approach: pretrained models that can make predictions on new datasets without task-specific training. Productionizing ML systems at scale remains a challenge for many enterprises for the following reasons: Recently, agentic solutions have helped accelerate these expensive operations, but they still rely on a bespoke-trained model for each ML task or dataset. To remove this dependency, pioneering research labs have applied the transformer architecture to tabular data at scale, creating a new category of models called Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs). Because TFMs come pretrained, they require no training on your dataset, meaning bespoke training and retraining pipelines largely disappear. Despite the impressive accuracy these models demonstrate on public benchmarks, they have not yet cracked into the mainstream of enterprise AI. This is partially due to the nascent nature of the field, as not many practitioners know about them yet, but also due to compute infrastructure requirements. In this article, we'll examine how TFMs work, compare recent models and explain the trade-offs involved in adopting them for enterprise ML. We'll then demonstrate how Databricks AI Runtime supports TFM experimentation and fine-tuning with managed GPU infrastructure, integrated development tools and model governance. TFMs largely eliminate the need for training and the overhead of maintaining bespoke models. They are pretrained on millions of diverse synthetic datasets so that they can infer relationships between variables in an unseen dataset. At prediction time, the labeled rows are passed as context alongside the rows to predict. Attention, the core of the transformer architecture, then relates each new row to those examples. Predictions are produced by a single forward pass, a process called in-context learning (ICL). While this zero-shot approach provides a powerful baseline out of the box, TFMs can also be fine-tuned. story|title:trustgraph acls that follow.content_excerpt: Policy-as-code for what AI agents produce: decide where an agent's output can go, based on what it read. Policy-as-code for what AI agents produce. Decide where your agent's output can go, based on what it read. Permission systems decide what an agent may read . They lose track the moment the agent writes something new. In May 2025, Invariant Labs showed a coding agent reading a user's private repositories and publishing what it found in a pull request on a public one, after it read a crafted issue. Every step was something the agent was allowed to do. Reading private code was fine. Opening a public pull request was fine. Nothing checked that the second came from the first. Taking away access does not fix this: the agent needs the private code to do its job. What is missing is a rule about where things derived from it may go. The same gap opens each time one agent hands its work to another: the restriction should follow the data through every step. You write one small policy file. It says who may read anything derived from each source, which agents may use it, and where each action sends output: TrustGraph records what each output was built from, through every step, and answers allow , needs approval or deny with the reason: Approval adds a requirement. It never widens who may read a source. Anything the policy does not name is denied. A policy carries its own tests. Each one states what the agent read, what it tries to do and the answer you expect. Read a policy back in plain English, see exactly who gains access when it changes, and run it through the simulator: Every command takes --json . There are six worked policies in examples/policies . TrustGraph assumes an agent drafts the policy and a person approves it. Every problem is reported at once with a path, a stable code and a suggestion, so an agent can run the loop init → check → test → simulate → explain → diff on its own. A person then reviews the plain-English explanation and a diff in which every widening of access is marked. Point your agent at docs/agents/writing-policies.md or llms.txt . Protect the policy file with code review. Status. The policy CLI, trustgraph serve and trustgraph gateway have been through security review; the gateway's assumptions are listed in docs/gateway.md . The Python integrations are not ready: four review rounds each found ways to drop a restriction, and their session handling is being rebuilt. Try them, but do not rely on them yet. story|title:why we rebuilt langsmith aro.content_excerpt: Last week we announced our series C and introduced the new LangSmith Agent Platform : a single place to build, run, improve, and govern every agent. With this, agents are now the core object across LangSmith, connecting fragmented workflows for developers and enabling platform teams to manage agents across the business. In this post, we discuss why we reorganized the product, how the agent model works, what it unlocks, and where we're taking it next. 2026 brought a step change in agent adoption as new harnesses , models, and engineering approaches made it possible to build agents that can reliably perform complex, high value work . Companies now run many agents across the business: engineering uses coding agents, product is building customer-facing agents, and teams across the organization have various internal productivity agents. These agents are built with different frameworks, hosted on various runtimes, and use a variety of tools and models. Engineers work across disconnected surfaces. Tracing , monitoring , and deployments all live in different places. This requires frequent context switching, and in practice results in teams skipping difficult but important steps like building the evals. AI Platform teams have difficulty answering basic governance questions. Which agents exist, and who owns each of them? What do they cost, and how are they performing? When costs spike, there is often no obvious person to ask what happened. We wanted to make it simple for teams to manage the entire agent development lifecycle from one place, using any stack, with ownership and governance across all of it. LangSmith supports the entire agent development lifecycle: build, run, improve, and govern. Now, we've connected the entire process through a unique agent record. When you open an agent record, its traces, evals, Agent Server, and Engine issues are accessible with one click, so you don’t need to navigate multiple surfaces to find them. Each agent’s local, dev, staging, and production environments sit under the same agent ID, so comparing performance after making changes is simple. LangSmith is composable, so you can choose the parts you need. If you already run your agent on another platform, you can connect it to LangSmith to improve and govern it without changing any other workflows.
